source.title: Attention-Based Prototypical Learning Towards Interpretable, Confident and Robust Deep Neural Networks

record.tranche_reason: The CIFAR-10 label-noise experiment reports test accuracy at several corruption levels, bearing on the test-performance portion of V4; it does not measure training error or reproduce the original random-label experiment.
record.gate_note: Table 3 reports test accuracy for three noisy-label ratios across three methods. It does not report training error, fitting of completely random labels, the zero-noise condition, or the all-noise condition. Other label-noise claims in the introduction and conclusion are not additional measured results.
record.test_reason: Table 3 tests V4's test-performance component: CIFAR-10 test accuracy decreases as random label corruption increases. It does not establish perfect training fit or memorization of the corrupted labels.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that sparsemax-based ProtoAttend improves robustness to label noise, and Table 3 reports higher test accuracy than baseline and dropout at each tested noise fraction.
record.recipe_differences: The study adds attention-based prototypical learning and compares methods on CIFAR-10 with partially corrupted labels; it does not apply the original random-label fitting experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: Label-noise ratio and method; the optimal sparsity regularization coefficient increases with higher noisy-label ratios.

fits_no_version.finding: ProtoAttend outperforms baseline and dropout on noisy-label test accuracy at all three tested corruption fractions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse prototype attention improves generalization under partial label corruption relative to these comparison methods.

record.problems: The label-noise results report test accuracy only, with no training accuracy or error, no uncertainty estimates, and only three noise ratios (0.4, 0.6, 0.8).
record.rows_left_out: No additional distinct results on the claim were reported. The robustness claim in the conclusion summarizes Table 3 rather than providing another result.

untested.parts: Fitting completely random labels to near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged training hyperparameters.
Relative time to fit true versus random labels and convergence slowdown with increasing corruption. Reported training budgets are separately optimized, not measured times to perfect fit.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

Perfect training fit throughout corruption levels, memorization of noise, and degradation across the full zero-to-all corruption range. Three intermediate noise levels cannot establish a smooth curve or its chance endpoint.
Whether explicit regularization prevents random-label fitting and whether removing it harms true-label generalization.
Whether shared real-data patterns are learned before noisy labels; no relevant training trajectories are reported.

missing.what: Extract the V4 test-accuracy results at noise fractions 0.4, 0.6, and 0.8: baseline 77.47, 71.27, 57.02%; dropout 78.99, 72.15, 56.76%; ProtoAttend 80.04, 74.67, 60.50%. These measure the test-error trend even though training fit is unreported. Learning rates, training budgets, dropout rates, and sparsity coefficients are optimized by condition; corrupted labels exclude the correct class.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. Missing training-error measurements leave the memorization component untested; they do not negate the reported test-error trend or justify a limits_scope verdict.

versions.untested_parts: No result reports fitting completely random labels, training error, or test error at chance.
No comparison of training time for true versus random labels or convergence speed across corruption fractions.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

Test accuracy at corruption ratios 0.4, 0.6, and 0.8 is reported, but training error is not. There is no zero-noise or all-noise result, and the text does not establish that training fit remains perfect.

The dropout method is compared on noisy-label test accuracy, but the study does not report whether dropout prevents fitting random labels or whether removing regularization harms generalization on true labels.
No result measures whether real-label patterns are learned before noisy or random labels.

relationships.condition: Test-performance component only; CIFAR-10 at corruption fractions 0.4, 0.6, and 0.8, for the baseline encoder, dropout, and ProtoAttend.
relationships.reason: From Table 3 text, with no extracted row ids: accuracy falls monotonically from 77.47 to 71.27 to 57.02% for baseline, 78.99 to 72.15 to 56.76% for dropout, and 80.04 to 74.67 to 60.50% for ProtoAttend. This supports increasing test error over the tested range.
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy declined successively from 77.47% to 71.27% to 57.02% for the baseline, 78.99% to 72.15% to 56.76% for dropout, and 80.04% to 74.67% to 60.50% for ProtoAttend.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
